comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Experimentally determined the cropped limits of the vertical dash. Tested various layouts and positioning with Alex. Collected font assets for Alex.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Tried idea to build modulus function from pure arithmetic. Idea seems correct but the dash software for some reason just spits out the default value above 9. Reverted back to image selector idea. Used paint to concatenate two images, could probably pump out the full image set in one to two hours but sounds prone to error. Looked up Python libraries to make images. Used OpenCV and a for loop to build all images 0-99 needed. Loaded first 25 and test drove on live hardware. Adjusted speed variable to use GPS instead of AEM speed. Concept works. Extended idea to 200+ images to check memory constraints. Downloads take a little time but everything fits and the dash boots.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Built static proof image of dash to show team. Organized development directory and purged messy / no working code bits. Re-visited python script to combine images. Ran script again for both big and little numbers. Loaded all 400+ image assets into the dash program. Tested downloads working correct with increased memory demands.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Analyzed script that ChatGPT gave me to understand how it was working. Modified script for loops to have 00-99 and 000-999 for the little numbers. Created new image assets and organized into working directory to load into AEMDash. Sat and clicked ~2000 times to load all image selectors.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Finished uploading all 500 images to the dash program. Replaced static screen images with dynamic image selectors. Manually typed in all scenarios to round 0-254 for range. Tested background colors and removed pink border from testing. Re-loaded all images assets provided by Alex to verify I was using the correct ones. Met with Alex to discuss charge screen.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued adding in numbers to the rounding function for range. Downloaded new image set from Alex. Replaced on screen objects. Used alignment template to position things properly.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Picked up where I left off loading in new image assets. Verified I as using the latest for everything. Finished typing in channel to round estimated range from float to integer. Loaded all the charge bar images & discovered program too large to download. Deleted images until the exact max file size was found, ~8kB. Discussion with Alex about getting smaller images. Tried various methods to reduce memory.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Loaded new charge bar images and calculated memory difference. ~850kB less which should give enough room to add back in some of the other features. Test downloaded. Everything fits now.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Reviewed all onscreen objects and verified each and everyone functional and matches expected value. Test drove to verify additional calibration points. Reduced Warning and Fault screens by 35% and moved into display area. Added in condensed diag screen with core items, checked everything transferred correctly. Validated charge screen pulling up reasonable estimates.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Loaded correct temperature bar and splash images. Adjusted width for power bar. Tested new idea to reduce clicks necessary to make an image selector. Started on image selector for pack voltage.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Finished uploading images for Pack Voltage on the charge screen. Ran into the memory limit again. Started stripping out non-essential images and re-trying loading until the dash boots.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Loaded correct RND images and tested in vehicle. Corrected dash version numbers. Removed background box used for alignment.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Located Dash program and reduced memory until it would load. Moved Pack Volts back on to the charge screen. That display channel now only shows odd numbers between 330V and 370V. Charged for a bit. Added gauges to the new gauge sheet.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Opened the portrait dash design file and got back up to speed on remaining items. Looked into how I was able to make the temperature slider work, it has 17 possible values going from 0 to 80 by 5. Closest I can get to 20 to 80 is 22 to 78 by 3.5. Inputing this is very tedious so I'm saving it for the start of a day.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Adjusted the temperature scale on the digital dash to better suit the type W motor. Added new channels and a lookup table for a 16 to 80 scaling. Added in all the new number ranges for the channel doing the rounding then went to update the image selector which turns out can't handle floating point. Went back to the tedious brute force input method. Battled program memory useage getting too high and the dash no longer booting. Removed some charge bar photos to resolve that. Tested the temperature slider on the bench with the gauges program, mostly working now. Worked to get the no data message to turn on and timeout correctly. Added in a change log and verified verion numbers correct on the boot and diag screens.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued digital dash work. Checked PRD was in the right order. Added Pack_Current to the charge screen by filling out another image selector with all the associated variables and logic to round and filter that signal. Tested charging to verify functionality. Ivanhoe showing 13% SOC now. Checked the total energy accum on the pack and multiplied that by the current SOC based on cell voltage alone. Added this new number to the energy counter and set that as the new PackMaxCapacity. Results show a change from 32,000 kWh to 38,000 kWh in comparison to the 36,000 kWh we ended up with in Berke.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Started on a more automated dash / gauges checkout program but couldn't really figure out a format that would work and be done today. Used Claude to organize all the signals that are used on the dash into a single DBC as a happy medium. Now I don't have to dig through a list with hundreds and hundreds of signals 41 times to fully validate a set of gauges or dash. Used new DBC with old gauges test program to verify the latest dash program. Fixed a few minor things and removed the temporary development widgets. Added in a PackVoltage image selector to the charge screen using a new MUCH easier dash technique I found. Still need to strip out any addition un-used pictures and load into the vehicle.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued loading the numbers from 300 to 405 one by one for the pack volts image selector. Stripped all un-used images from the file saving some memory which puts the dash further away from where it instantly doesn't boot. Loaded the program into the vehicle and verified the basics working as expected.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Methodically walked through all the widgets for the main screen and charge screen substituting values and watching how they worked on screen. Corrected various issues along the way. Completed 11/13 of the complicated widgets.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Finished checking the various widgets while taking thorough status notes. Loaded the screen to the vehicle and gave a basic look over. Posted notes to Slack.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Ivanhoe Alfa Dash: Finished checking widgets and making any improvements along the way. Thoroughly documented all the backend work and posted to Slack. Developed new logic for PND which still need to be better tested on a dry day. Fed a bunch of screen shots of DashDesign to Claude and developed a list of everything that makes the Warning and Fault lamps trigger. Collected other resources and built a prompt that resulted in a test tool that send CAN messages like the VCU would but without having to sit down and reason what each value should be and then go find it somewhere in a giant list. Used the tool to check warning and fault lamps. Wrote up summary of the day.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Troubleshooting for BMS fault now showing on the dash and gauges. Disabled fault reporting for thermistor channels BMSM1_G03_Therm3 & BMSM1_G06_Therm3 since they seemed way out of range (disconnected) and were causing a BMS fault. comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Loaded the Berke calibration into the vehicle. Started charging the vehicle up to the top but not getting current for some reason. Found many checkout items haven't been looked at. Ran through the entire checkout sheet from top to bottom and added items to the formatted punch list. Posted for team.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Already had a Berke firmware migration installed, reviewed the delta an found ~20 differences. Flashed the latest Berke firmware burn and updated gear ratio and pedal calibration, and pack capacity. Added all these changes into the tracking sheet. Reviewed completeness in the rest of the sheet. Need to at a minimul check the inverter settings.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified energy counters messed up due to incorrect current direction. Inverted the IVT direction and left on charge.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text:
Reviewed compare reports again between Berke and Ivanhoe. Produced a list of required differences and what those configuration options should be for Ivanhoe. Checked energy counters, still massively off after one charge cycle. Reflashed Berke Rev5 firmware burn to get the "reset" option. Transfered the compare report settings in. Verified everything set correctly, backed up this calibrations and sent off to AEM for a firmware burn. Charged to the top alongside watching energy counters, pack resistance, etc. making sure everything looked within reason. Couldn't average the CellR values like I usually do since the pack was too high but the initial calculation was within spec. Clicked through the digital dash making note problems due to the VCU200_15 build with an Elcon charger and DCDC, as well as portrait layout oddities. Test drove verifying top end limiters. The digital dash doesn't have a logger but I manually pulled the logs and used my existing scripts to convert to CSV. Imported the logs for plotting and verified the limiters plot looked consistent with the cell specs. Made final backups of the inverter and PMU. Flashed the firmware burn and left on charge.

For review, here's the Berke To Ivanhoe Delta

        APP2_Min        0.560        0.570
        DriveGearRatio        4.10        4.56
        DriveTireDiameter        23.44        24.80
        PackCurrentPolarity        Invert        ---
        PackMaxCapacity        36000        32000

        Get wifi credentials, upload, verify configuration sync'd.
        Finish Digital Dash (Remove EGT/CCU readings, Add charge confirmation, Correct portrait visual problems)
        Test drive, verify lower limiters, make plots for pack consumption, temps, & low limiters.
        Verify running temps and InvTempRefOption.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued Dash work. Removed more image assets to give a little more memory headroom. Used Claude to make an additional image asset to properly label the pack current channel. Loaded this and tested for boot stability. Added in missing message for low SOC warning. Tested gauges to make sure warning light came on in various scenarios. Verified PackMaxCapacity was set up higher, test drove and checked limiters. Sent firmware off to AEM for a second burn.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Flashed the firmware burn, checked various options looked correct, left on the charger overnight.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Organized and reduced the ten or so partial efforts to convert and decode logs. Ended up with single well organized directory with tools compatible with our logger that AI could use to properly digest data. Organized DBC files specific to AEM and copied them over to the Conversion Tools directory changing their format as required. Manually downloaded logs from the CANcloud for the charge the evening of July 7th and manually ran them through the conversion process. This conversion process is now setup correctly to have AI repeat without ever getting the "Oh you're right, good for you to push back" instead of garbage presented as fact. Fed all the previous into an open conversation and had Claude build a report of the failure. Reviewed analysis and posted for the team.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Re-downloaded the logs from yesterday and added in some additional logs to make sure that the recharge was captured, Converted these and gave them to Claude along with AEM manuals, an exported calibration, and additional context about how this charger works. Went back and forth evaluating and dismissing various theories proposed based off of actual experience with what option does what and what parts of logic in the VCU don't work and are bypassed on purpose. Built a CSV plotter with the log data, clicked around a little bit and ultimately became very concerned about how basic plots don't look as expected. Told this to Claude & continued discussing with the team. Ultimately decided the charge not starting is not a problem.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued back and forth with Claude and various Slack correspondence with Marc.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: (Last night) Built a log replay script with Claude to get the CSS logs into the AEM format for analysis. (Today) Tested the log replay script which crashed immediatly. Let Claude debug everything with actual hardware in auto mode. Got everything working and tested the process to get a CSS log into AEMData. All looked good so I set the whole charge failure to play back at 10x speed while logging, overloaded the bus. Will setup to run over night and check back in tomorrow.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued work on the log replay tool. Added a way to change the playback speed and worked on the display setup to be logging all the critical channels. Tried logging but started getting bus overload errors with CAN2 and CAN3 merged.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Setup the log playback tool with 1M baud to hopefully eliminate bus overload issues. Played back the very start of the log and got useable results. Let run for a while to get a fuller log to test. Removed not applicable items from the diag screen and verified logic and CAN messages associated with the gauges, couldn't get the VCU turned off with the digital dash still turned on to test the signal chain. Trying alternative methods tomorrow.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued diag and correspondence with AEM. Used Claude to better understand the problem & analyzed plots on my own. Decided there's nothing more we can do about the issue.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Test drove to verify mileage. Ran through drive modes to verify PND on the dash. Updated the change log and version info in the dash and re-downloaded. Scaled the power bar and verified. Ran through the checklist & updated on Slack. Added in a firmware reset detection mechanism and the images in the dash to make that work. Tested. During testing found a reliable way to force a weak charge. Repeated this procedure until I caught it on a log. Analyzed and posted to Slack.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Installed correct C2Prog version for flashing AEM LDU boards. Flashed firmware 6B33. Compared the symbols files I'm using for backups between 6B28 thru 6B33. They all match exactly. Used Claude to compare EEPROM. Setup a directory with the 3 stock EEPROM files as well as the Ampere provided, the Icon Bronco, and the previous Blazer. Fed Claude prompts and inspected output till something very copy and pastable was produced, checked each setting line by line and then flashed into this LDU. Marked all inverter parts on the sheet N/A where the don't line up because of the different motor type. Inverter checkout now 100%.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Built longer PMU programming harness to avoid PSU balancing act. Disconnected PMU's from vehicle, and upgraded both their firmwares to the latest. Looked up which PMU software revision we were on and flashed those calibrations to each. Hooked up Raptor-Service and key'd on to an immediate CAN1 crash. Will need to investigate vehicle basics like CAN termination tomorrow.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Started diag on CAN1 crashing. Checked CAN termination on all networks. CAN3 and BMS CAN both missing one resistor. Discovered PMU's no longer waking up properly. Pulled open doc for the power block and verified MPR relay connections. Measured GND where 12V should actually be, discussed both issues with Brandon, Billy, and Alex and found the GUI needed to be plugged in and one critical connector to the rear battery box was pinned the wrong gender. Swept and mopped the grease and machine chips scattered around the truck.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Picked backup after connector issue last week. Verified PMUs booting properly now and all CAN networks were terminated correctly. Filled out that section of the checkout sheet. Connected to Raptor-Service and pulled a configuration backup from the VCU. Noticed BMS configuration hadn't made it to the VCU. Tried forcing this from Raptor-Service but was locked out. Checked all faults and there's a bunch including ole BattWakeFault. Measured BMS CAN traffic and found 100% with many error per second. Checked for BMS CAN High / Low swap at all three boxes, didn't see anything but the wiring is extra tight.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Watched the VCU, PMU, and BMS CAN simultaneously while trying to enable the battery system. Looks like the battery wake signal never makes it to the BMS or even the PMU. Checked a few outputs on one PMU to determine PMU1 and PMU2 were flipped. Corrected that and cleared faults. Pumps turned on for a moment, topped off coolant. Keycycled and the pumps stopped, now getting an HVIL fault. Diagnosed that back to the CCS box and HVJB box connectors being swapped. Disassembled that enough to get access to the connector. Re-assembled and cleared faults, VCU seems to be stable now. Troubleshot GUI rebooting every 1/2 second, will need more access to that to continue.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Wrote up finding from yesterdays work. Verified all backups in correct directory and all notes made it to the checkout sheet. Cleaned up cable mess around vehicle.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Downloaded new VCU release and fully read through the change notes. Made a Raptor-Service tab that has all the tags for values that get reset during a firmware flash. Flashed the new VCU firmware release 1.8.4 and checked over the configuration. Adjusted to match checkout sheet. Grabbed logger from pile, verified configuration backup and installed. Verified HVIL now working correctly. Troubleshot pedal out of range fault, still only reading 0-30%. Got the GUI to boot by re-seating a jammed & crooked connector. Unflipped the constant and switched power to the GUI. Cleaned up and checked off punch list items.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified APP min and max for Connolly and Barton. Ran the same test in Preheim to compare. Preheim definitly has APP channel 1 and APP channel 2 swapped. Installed APK 2.5.0, Dash 2.1, and XML V36. Configured the autolaunch app in settings. Tested GUI boot and it all seems to be working well.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified APP is now seeing 100%, test drove the truck finally. Noticed some mechanical issues like a spongy brake and a shooshooshoo sound. Kept getting a fault for DCDCVoltXChk and ChgPortContFlt when we tried charging. Added various new issues to the punchlist and opened a ticket to Ampere for them.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Troubleshot gear selection issue with Billy. Checked PRND, BrakeSwitch, IMD, HVIL, etc. in Raptor-Service. Nothing wrong could be found, VCU seemed to simply not be running logic. Re-flashed firmware and issue went away.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Built an AEMDash screen to show a similar view to the ECUMaster software, but with some flexibility on view and no control to incorrectly alter the program. Dusted off my collection of PMU CAN integration notes and programs and looked for a good donor candidate to pull the CAN configuration out of. Imported this configuration to get back to the spot I was when developing on Buck and having CAN bus crashing issues. Realized again that ECUMaster Export changes input to outputs and output to inputs. Rebuilt the Output_Status messages with the proper direction for PMU1. Reloaded the other PMU programs so the truck is still driveable.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued adding messages into the PMU CAN Interface DBC for PMU2. Manually copied these over into the PMU for a number of the messages. Ran through five or so points in the PMU checkout process, corrected fans that would never turn on. Still need to verify some non critical points like cabin heat and lights and then all the more dangerous points like HV contactors, which I was unwilling to do with Billy physically shaking the vehicle side to side.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Loaded the PMU CAN Interface version of logic matricies so I wouldn't have to re-check all outputs to continue development on that. Re-checked the several channels I had done previously. Ran through the rest of the channels including cabin heat. Marked notes and punch list items that where found. All IO is good except for the AC and heat related ones, as well as the reverse lights and EPAS sensor. Improved my Raptor-Service tab for PMU checkout. Made new logic matrix for the PMU CAN revisions, added in comments and marked changes in red. Removed some spare channels. Verified current trip settings and input voltage hysteresis settings. Corrected the few that were slightly off. Took note of all input voltages as I ran through the whole checkout list and changed their threshold to 1.5/2.5V to increase their error margin. Reviewed vehicle requirements doc and converted that into a VCU configuration. Checked settings in the VCU. Set the battery cell type to a 155Ah cell since there's not a 147Ah one available. Asked Ampere about adding this 6S-2P cell to the firmware. Weighed the vehicle and put the numbers into the GUI. Verified they made it to the VCU. Ran through the punch list marking off items and posted open items to Slack. Ran through checkout sheet marking off previous items as skipped. Vehicle now at 78% progress, has moved from checkout to testing, and has a green card.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Tested old negative contactor. Definitely welded. Hooked up a meter to the output of the junction box and verified that the 25 Ohm precharge and discharge resistors were not blown. Verified contactor replacement cycling without MSD. Disabled high voltage via Ampere's "HVdisable" and verified vehicle had no faults. Plugged in MSD. Started up vechile and sucessfully put into gear.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued evening Slack discussion.

comments.author: Devin DuMont

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Updated all the firmwares and configurations and re-tried charging, no luck. The charger itself is much simpler and doesn't have a lot of built-in diagnostics but we figure it's not seeing the pack voltage. We should check if the charger fuse is blown or maybe a HV pin isn't terminated quite correctly. Then definitely make sure the polarity is not reversed.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Worked with Billy to confirm that pack voltage was not seen at the onboard charger. Determined there was a blown fuse, had him replace that. Troubleshot Raptor-Service repeatedly crashing after ~30 seconds of use, deleted extra & similar firmware versions from the repository but still couldn't get a solid connection to the VCU established. Asked Andrew about a potential firmware bug, moved on. Plugged in and verified charging was now working. Loaded latest PMU software from Witham with the heater controls included. Immediatly got a terrible sounding relay and had to disable. Reviewed logic compatibility with HVAC doc, it was not compatible with more than just a blower powered from a PWM blower output. Changed this to Ignition and re-worked how the master branch climate controls work in the PMU. Opened ticket to enable correct heater option in VCU.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Transfered over firmware files from Summit and verified the Raptor-Service crashing issue was gone. Enabled the cabin heater option in the VCU and ran through the PMU heater controls again. Found awful buzzing sound when using PWM again. Determined actual wiring did not match the PMU comments. Talked to Billy for more information and drew climate controls schematic from the HVAC document. Added in information not captured in HVAC document or diagram. Adjusted controls in vehicle, will need to determine better strategy to have universal PMU program.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Hooked up to PMU while Andrew hooked up to the VCU. Slid the fan and temp sliders back and forth monitoring signals to the PMU and signals to the VCU. Determined a theory on the wiring and desired control scheme, stopped there to clarify some questions with the team.

comments.author: Devin DuMont

comments.author: Devin DuMont

@channel OK, I drove it. Definitely still vibration, though. I used the vibration app on my phone on the floor of the car and found two peaks. One at 12Hz and one at 24Hz when I was driving at about 50 mph. These tires turn 870 revs per mile so, at 50mph, that's about 725rpm. 725rpm/60 seconds = 12Hz.  If it were driveshaft vibration, it would be at 4.1x wheel speed which is 2972rpm and about 49.5Hz.  So, I believe we are dealing with wheel vibration here

Let's have our best shop re-balance these wheels @Ryan Laurel and, if it's still there, we can tell Pat that we can try to get a set of these but no guarantee that they'll be perfect either:

www.niemoeller.de/en/w180/w180/B010/26/c40004-disc-wheel-with-drop-centre-rim-5jx13 
 from our collective brain:
The two cursors land on two different things.
Cursor 1 at 11.8 Hz = 708 rpm. That's your wheel/tire rotation. At 50 mph and 870 rev/mile you computed 725 rpm = 12.1 Hz, so 11.8 Hz is dead-on (within speedometer/tire-circumference slop). This is first-order tire/wheel imbalance — a heavy spot or out-of-balance wheel hitting once per revolution. It shows up strongest on X (fore-aft) and Z, consistent with an imbalance/uniformity issue.
Cursor 2 at 23.7 Hz = 2× the wheel frequency, the second harmonic. A peak at exactly twice rotation speed is the classic signature of tire/wheel non-uniformity — radial force variation, out-of-round, a flat spot, or a mounted-tire/rim runout that produces two bumps per revolution. It's the dominant peak in your X trace, which fits a radial uniformity problem felt as a fore-aft/vertical shake.
So what's going on: you've got a wheel-speed-order vibration. 1st order (11.8 Hz) points to imbalance, and a strong 2nd order (23.7 Hz) points to tire uniformity / out-of-round / runout. Both scale with vehicle speed, so the give-away test is to drive at a different speed — both peaks should slide proportionally (e.g., at 60 mph they'd move to ~14.2 and ~28.4 Hz). If they move with speed, it's rotational and not engine/driveline-fixed or structural resonance.
A couple of things worth checking to confirm and narrow it down:
The smaller red bump near ~3 Hz (around 180 rpm) — too slow for the tire; could be a driveshaft or half-shaft order depending on your axle ratio, or body/suspension hop. Worth identifying since your build has a custom driveline.
Whether the 23.7 Hz peak dominates over 11.8 Hz (it does here, in X) suggests the uniformity/out-of-round issue is the bigger contributor to what you feel than raw imbalance.
Practical next step: road-force balance or at least a spin balance plus a runout check on the worst wheel. If balancing kills the 11.8 Hz but leaves 23.7 Hz, the tire itself (or the rim) has a uniformity defect and may need to be re-indexed on the rim or replaced.

well ... i went deeper ... and told it "this really only happens around 50mph" ... and the answer is quite interesting (if true)

Here's the distinction. Imbalance and uniformity peaks (your 11.8 and 23.7 Hz) are always present; their amplitude grows smoothly with speed and never has a "sweet spot" where it gets bad and then better. What you're describing — bad at 50, better on either side — means that at 50 mph, a rotational forcing frequency is lining up with the natural frequency of some part of the car, and that part is ringing.
At 50 mph your tire turns at 11.8 Hz (1st order) and the 2nd order sits at 23.7 Hz. One of those is almost certainly coinciding with a structural resonance:
23.7 Hz is a very typical tire/suspension hop or wheel-hop resonance (unsprung mass on the tire/suspension spring rate usually lands in the 12–18 Hz range, but bushing-stiffened or heavier custom setups push higher). It's also right in the band for many driveshaft bending modes and subframe modes.
The fact that the 23.7 Hz peak is the dominant one in your X trace, and the symptom is speed-specific, strongly suggests the 2nd tire order is exciting a structure that resonates around there.
So the mechanism: the tire's 2nd-order force (from uniformity/out-of-round) is the exciter, and something on the car has a natural frequency near 23.7 Hz that amplifies it. Off 50 mph, the forcing frequency walks away from the resonance and the amplitude drops. That's why it's a 50 mph phenomenon and not a 40 or 60 phenomenon.

Connolly 220S — vibration diagnosis (July 7)
Diagnostic steps taken today:
Re-measured vibration after roadforce balancing + re-clocking the wheels. The 2nd-order "out-of-round wheel" signature dropped ~75% (wheels were a real, now largely-fixed contributor), but a once-per-rev (1st-order) vibration remained and became dominant. Balancing can't touch that, so it points inboard to the hub/flange — matching Dave's damaged pass-rear flange reading .007–.009" lateral runout.
Cleared a separate scraping noise: cotter-pin wire diameter too small, letting the spring keeper rub inside the drum. Confirmed the flange damage was pre-existing (visible in earlier brake-work photos).
Jackstand test, driveline spun bare (no wheels/tires/drums, ~55–60 mph equiv): pulling the wheels + drums removed ~70% of total vibration (0.110 → 0.031 g). Confirmed most of it lives at the wheel/tire/drum/flange interface, but exposed a smaller driveshaft 1st-order residual (~0.013 g) that wheel work won't fix.
Axle isolation test, each rear axle spun alone (open diff, opposite side held): right axle threw a big once-per-rev shake (0.039 g) vs the left (0.002 g) — ~20x worse. A clean 1st order like that is the signature of a bent/eccentric right rear axle shaft or flange.
Final conclusion: the right rear axle is bent — that's the residual vibration source; the left axle is good. It's one axle, not the pair, so the ~$7,500 German set isn't needed. Plan: confirm with a dial indicator (right vs. left as reference), re-face the flange for brake-drum seating, and source/refurbish a used right axle. Next steps: order a 2nd-hand right axle plus wheel bearing, pull the RH axle and take both to a machine shop; if the old one measures true, the issue is deeper in the diff (possibly u-joint). Colvin's was called for input before pulling on-site.

Angle from tube to case:
Ride height: 2.0-2.5 degrees (axle pointed up).
At jackstand level: ~6 degrees

Got another vibration measurement at 60mph. Marc put into Claude. Results:
U-joint / ride-height experiment — it split the problem in two
Re-ran the right-axle jackstand test, but this time loaded the car so the swing-axle U-joint was straight (yesterday it was bent because unloaded).
Confirmed — U-joint angle drives the 2nd-order vibration. A Cardan joint at an angle makes a twice-per-rev shake. Straightening it dropped the 2nd-order component 87% (0.0083 → 0.0011 g). So ride height genuinely matters — setting/holding correct static ride height removes a real chunk of vibration. Cheap win.
But the main defect is 1st-order and it did NOT move. The right axle's once-per-rev shake stayed put (0.042 → 0.035 g, within speed variation). A U-joint angle can't cause a 1st-order — that's a bent shaft / eccentric flange / imbalance. So the joint isn't the cause of the big one; it's mechanical, and it travels with the right axle.
Road implication worth noting: on the road the U-joint's 2nd-order lands at ~29 Hz — the same frequency we've been calling "out-of-round wheel." So part of that stubborn 28.6 Hz on the road was probably the U-joint running at an angle, which is why roadforce balancing never fully killed it. Fixing ride height should take another bite out of it.
Two separable issues on the right rear now:
1. U-joint operating angle (ride height) — real, 2nd-order, fixable by geometry. Set + verify static ride height. Experiment shows it works.
2. Right axle 1st-order defect — bent shaft / eccentric joint flange (part 27) / imbalance. This is the main event. Dial-indicate the right axle shaft + flange runout vs the left as reference, and check the U-joint (part 6) for wear/play while we're in there.
Caveat: jackstand spins the right axle at 2x road speed, so it exaggerates the 1st-order force ~4x. Real defect, but the road contribution is more modest than the number here (it's the ~14 Hz road residual, ~0.03 g).
Plan: dial in ride height, then measure/address the right axle shaft + flange runout. New wheels still won't touch either of these.

comments.text:
Work performed
The right rear axle and a new wheel bearing were ordered first thing. Marc's ride-height experiment split the vibration in two: straightening the U-joint angle killed the 2nd-order shake by 87% (fixable via ride height), but the main 1st-order defect stayed — a mechanical fault traveling with the right axle. David then inspected the internal U-joint and found it clearly bad: excessive play, lash, witness marks, notchiness. He made the car drivable again (gear oil, parking brake, wheels torqued). Jordan mapped the parts across German fiches (sliding joint 1803500513, U-joint 111 350 00 28, sliding sleeve, shims) — ~$1,600 to rebuild, or ~$450 for a used U-joint — and located a needed special tool.
Communications made
Internally, the team agreed to call Casey at Colvin's for a removal/rebuild plan; Jordan noted he'd specifically asked Colvin's to check this joint during the original rebuild and it apparently wasn't. Externally, you sent two supplier emails: one to Jelinek ("1959 220S") asking for part 53/53A from a rear-axle diagram, and one to Niemöller ("W180 rear axle sliding joint compatibility question") asking them to confirm sliding sleeve 180 350 07 13 fits your car.
Conclusions
Two separable issues: a ride-height/U-joint angle component (fixable by geometry) and the main 1st-order defect, now pinned largely on a worn internal U-joint that should have been caught in the prior rebuild. Next step is a gameplan call with Colvin's, with parts sourcing pending replies from the two German suppliers. The car is drivable meanwhile.

Comment from yesterday:
"Installed rear shocks.
Attempted to adjust rear ride height.
Issues with vintage v-dubs IRS kit were discovered when attempting to adjust rear ride height.
Welds failing on swing plates adjustment blocks.
Torsion bar side of the adjustable swing plate not properly constrained to the backing plate, causing the plates to walk apart as the suspension moved. When I adjusted the screw this time it actually split the two apart completely. From the marks on the adjuster plate it looks to have been walking for a while.
The old shocks showed evidence of contact with the trailing arm.
Did a bunch of research to determine the best path going forward. As much as I'd just like to buy new spring plates and be done with it, they appear to be custom to this application and though I can find lots of parts that look similar I'm unable to determine compatibility. Every kit maker does this part a little differently. So we're best off fixing what we have.Had @Aharon Adams take a look at everything since he has the most torsion bar experience.
Plan going forward:
Remove spring plates. Straighten the plate and re-weld the adjustment blocks.
Add constraining hardware to ensure the two-part plate can't pull apart. The slot is there, but no matching stud or thread on the companion plate. Looking around it does appear to be something most high-quality kits do.
Add a bushing to the torsion bar cap to press the two plates together. This wasn't included in the kit but Aharon confirmed it's a necessity.
Install a longer adjustment screw to give us a little more height.
Regarding the shock mounting, I believe one of the many parts that were missing from the kit was upper shock mounts which were likely to prevent this contact. Where the shock mounts were intended to go I'm not sure. I moved the spacers around to create maximum clearance, and it appears that currently it will not make contact at full droop. Once we start driving it we can see if we need to address this. On the lift it seems OK."

Summary from today:
Unable to adjust ride height, and during arm replacement observed the torsion leaf stack ends no longer square. Attempted removal of torsion leaves for inspection: unable to remove leaves, jammed. Eventually able to hammer torsion leaves out and discovered the central keeper had stretched apart to the point where the torsion leaf stack had rotated and was no longer fully constrained in the center. This likely explains the crappy ride and, only the upper torsion leaf stack was actually supporting the weight, the lower stack was doing almost nothing. The upper torsion bar keeper was still intact, but was also stretching. And one final note, there are actually two leaves missing from each stack. Not sure if vintage v-dubs miscounted, or if they did that to change the spring rate. I'm going to add in the missing leaves when I reinstall.
I spoke with Nate a Wagenwest. He is rush shipping us a set of new central keepers. He actually said the slit is necessary for the torsion leaves to settle properly, but that the quality of the metal was very important. He asked where I got the beam from, and his response: "I could have guessed that"... he described vintage v-dubs as a bad company with "a long history of disasters". No surprise there...
As soon as the keepers come in I will put the front end back together.

This likely explains the crappy ride and, only the upper torsion leaf stack was actually supporting the weight, the lower stack was doing almost nothing. The upper torsion bar keeper was still intact, but was also stretching. And one final note, there are actually two leaves missing from each stack. Not sure if vintage v-dubs miscounted, or if they did that to change the spring rate. I'm going to add in the missing leaves when I reinstall.
I spoke with Nate a Wagenwest. He is rush shipping us a set of new central keepers. He actually said the slit is necessary for the torsion leaves to settle properly, but that the quality of the metal was very important. He asked where I got the beam from, and his response: "I could have guessed that"... he described vintage v-dubs as a bad company with "a long history of disasters". No surprise there...
As soon as the keepers come in I will put the front end back together.

comments.text:
spent the day deliberating and choosing a path forward.
I ended up straightening all the bent plates from the drivers side
Then tapping both slide plates to m12 so we can have a better clamping force.
While installing the torsion plates, I evened both sides at 9cm- spring plate to corner of the housing. I then preloaded the arms while sliding them in and securing.
After that I could pull the arms over to meet the slide plates and realign to the previous spots.
This method insures our "lowest" ride height is also the lowest position on the adjuster, now we can go way up if we want.
After we decide we like our ride height, we will remove the wheels and add 2 extra bolts towards the end of the spring plates, that way we can lock it down permanently and not worry about the plates deforming any more.

comments.author: Jordan Jones
comments.text:
Front wheel spacers have been removed. With the new set of front suspension components we had a new situation where with Billy and I in the front while turning right hard we could get the front of the left tire to rub the fender. Removing the spacers greatly reduced that except at the most extreme angle (me+Billy+full lock + torque on the wheel). Spacers were added long ago to prevent rear left tire-to-rear body contact. That no longer appears to be an issue with the new suspension height/spindles.

We will need to switch back to shorter wheel studs to fit the hubcaps. But I'll wait till we get an alignment done to make sure there isn't anything else that crops up when everything gets straightened out. It's also possible the minor rubbing that still exists will no longer be an issue.
